claim: Twice a day, an Antarctic ice stream lurches with about a magnitude-7 quake's strength.

start.title: Glacier
start.description: Persistent body of ice that moves downhill under its own weight

end.title: Whillans Ice Stream
end.description: Glaciological feature of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet

knots.passage: In glaciated areas where the glacier moves faster than one km per year, glacial earthquakes occur. These are large scale earthquakes that have seismic magnitudes as high as 6.1.
knots.hatnote: Glaciers flow, but fast ones don't always flow smoothly.

knots.passage: Since glacial earthquakes produce large amplitude and long period waves that deviate from traditional tectonic earthquake activity, glacial earthquakes require different monitoring methods. This is a primary reason why the specific class of glacial earthquakes was not discovered until 2003. Additionally, glacial earthquakes differ from tectonic earthquakes by lasting longer; for example, a tectonic earthquake with a magnitude of 5 may last 5 seconds, while a glacial earthquake with a magnitude of 5 may last 30 seconds.
knots.hatnote: These are earthquakes that look nothing like earthquakes.

knots.passage: Seismic waves are also generated by the Whillans Ice Stream, a large, fast-moving river of ice pouring from the West Antarctic Ice Sheet into the Ross Ice Shelf. Scientists found that each day, two seismic waves are released, each with strength equal to about a magnitude 7 earthquake.
knots.hatnote: Not classed with those quakes, one Antarctic ice stream still outdoes them.

knots.passage: The data show that the river of ice moves about a half-meter within approximately 30 minutes, remains still for 12 hours, then moves another half-meter in phase with gravitational tides. Each time it moves, it emits seismic waves that are recorded at seismographs around Antarctica and even as far away as Australia, a distance of more than 6,400 kilometers. In 2024, it was shown that the large slow seismic events on the ice stream cause the adjoining Ross Ice Shelf to abruptly shift by up to 6 cm in the course of a few minutes as trapped seismic waves within the shelf propagate northward.
knots.hatnote: And it runs on a timetable set by the tides.

payoff: A river of ice lurches with the tides twice a day, sending waves to Australia and jolting the whole Ross Ice Shelf.
caveats: 'Equivalent to a magnitude 7' describes the energy of slow slip events, not violent shaking like a tectonic quake.
